title: Terra Ignota
summary: Audacious, strange, and doused in philosophy

content.value: I have begun to realise that what I appreciate most in an author is
audacity

. Arkady Martine, who let us live within a culturally alien empire that believes utterly in its own narratives. Tamsyn Muir, who wove a perfect web using the impossible ingredients of the Bible, internet memes, and grief. Steven Erikson, crafting a hundred thousand years of tragedy to stare haggardly at us from within the pages.
I think Ada Palmer is the most audacious of them all. I think she knows it, too.
The acknowledgements of the final book in the series,
Perhaps The Stars

, implore us not to read it too soon. That we should take time to mull over the climax and bask in its glow. Then when you read the acknowledgements they too are audacious, a thematic continuation, a conclusion, an Acknowledgment. The reason I am writing strangely is that I am trapped inside the literary style of Ada Palmer and cannot escape until I finish this review.
Our modern moths have bounced so many times off lightbulbs, they aren’t prepared for torches, and forget that wings can burn.

The narrator of these books is unreliable. He will tell you so himself, repeatedly. He talks directly to you, and sometimes you talk back, and sometimes Thomas Hobbes is there as well, because why not. When I began this series I had not read anything about it (and if at this point my review has already convinced you, then go! Read it! Return afterward!) so I was expecting something resembling a normal sci-fi book. I came to realise over time (but slower than I should have) that the characters were not meant to be people. They were meant to be concepts, arguments, and philosophies. This is a book that wants you to think. The upside of being a concept rather than a human is that almost everyone is so very
reasonable

, world leaders and enemies collaborate for the greater good, no one breaks their oaths, and everyone is in service to a greater idea or symbol rather than selfishness or greed. Somehow, this doesn’t make the characters feel any less complex - in part, I think, because it is unclear whether this is really what the world is like, or if we are reading a stylised version of events presented by an insane narrator.
Oh, miraculous chameleon, science, who can reverse your doctrine hourly and never shake our faith! What cult ever battered by this world of doubt can help but envy you?

The world of 2454 has modelled itself on the culture and language of the Age of Enlightenment (or was it just our narrator reflecting himself on the world?) and while you may end up desiring to brush up on your Hobbes and Voltaire, the core arguments are familiar to anyone. Why must we endure Death, Distance, and Time? Does God exist, and what would He answer to the trolley problem? Should we reach for the stars, or should we first mend our home planet? It’s a mercy that the thematic core is fairly grounded, because the incredibly strange setting  falls somewhere between allegory and nonsensical. The Freemasons have taken over a fifth of the world, declared all Masonic conspiracy theory to be true, and have now taken on the thematic trappings of the Roman Empire. A Gundam style mech turns up at one point for a deus ex machina (a character notes that it’s a deus ex machina!). There’s a nation of mind-reading psychologists and another one of space-faring dragon riders. Anything can and will happen, because God may or may not be real.
The protagonist of every work of fiction is Humanity, and the antagonist is God.

The character the series (eventually) centers around is J.E.D.D MASON, whose entire nature I would consider a spoiler. In some ways I relate to him, perhaps because one of his names is Mike, (although it is short for Micromegas rather than Michael)
- but then, Tai-kun is canonically just a name rather than taikun, “Great Lord”, so similarly we must reference Michael, “Who Is Like God”? -

, but perhaps because sometimes I too feel like an incomprehensible alien. As, perhaps, do you. He is the strangest part of the book, partly because he’s not actually that strange (in that I’m sure I could find a real person who is stranger) but everyone within the text acts like he’s an alien.
War is the thesis that there is a special time when causing death is normal, legal, heroic, accepted, right; I Hate this thesis and I cannot call it justice.

Complaints about this book largely fall under moral or worldbuilding inconsistencies.  J.E.D.D MASON generally seems to lack agency, emotional maturity, and some types of abstract reasoning, yet the characters in the book believe he is perfect in every way. In the book’s core conflict of going to space vs investing in immortality, Palmer is clearly extremely in favour of the former. The prose presents the space-faring group called Utopia as being powerful, noble and fierce, while they consistently fail to articulate anything more convincing to justify their place as the Good Guys other than “go to space, ???, utopia” (to paraphrase). Each nation is often just as 2-dimensional and driven by thematic symbolism as the characters. In any other book this would be quite a concern. In this one it feels natural.
This series is for people who are interested in a sci-fi book doused in philosophy, theology, and a lot of weirdness.

alt: The cover of Perhaps the Stars by Ada Palmer, showing a futuristic moon base in the foreground, with the Earth hanging huge and imposing in the shadowy background.

title: Machineries of Empire
summary: A fabulously unique sci-fi world.

content.value: This is a really interesting sci-fi series, largely because the world Yoon Ha Lee depicts bears very little resemblance to our own. This is obvious right from the opening of the book:

At Kel Academy, an instructor had explained to Cheris's class that the threshold winnower was a weapon of last resort, and not just for its notorious connotations. Said instructor had once witnessed a winnower in use. The detail that stuck in Cheris's head wasn't the part where every door in the besieged city exhaled radiation that baked the inhabitants dead. It wasn't the weapon's governing equations, or even the instructor's left eye, damaged during the attack, from which ghostlight glimmered.
Ah yes, the
“threshold winnower”
. My favourite weapon.
Ghostlight
, of course. However, at this point I was still thinking that it might be a normal sci-fi book. Maybe this was jargon that would get explained soon.
Nope.

According to the briefing, the Eels have a directional storm generator. The storms scrambled vectors. The effect was localized, but it was troublesome when parallel columns ended up at opposite ends of a road a hundred kays apart [...].
Here I realised that this was
not

a normal sci-fi book. There’s an abnormal amount of math happening, and none of it’s explained. Yoon Ha Lee is too cool for such things as “exposition” and “info-dumps”. This can make things hard, sometimes. He has a degree in mathematics, which presumably is used to make all the equations and terms thrown around  - “fractal coefficient”, “modulo congruences” - believable. I certainly have no idea what most of them mean.

There isn’t any magic in the fantasy sense, there’s magic in the ‘sufficiently advanced technology’ sense, which is an interesting approach. The system hinges on ‘calendars’, a social order of observances and castes underpinned by more maths. A fervently religious adherence to the calendar is necessary to keep the magic working. Unfortunately, the calendar tends to involve torturing people and ruthlessly destroying anyone who dissents (for instance, by turning them into paper swans. This series is odd). The problem with vanquishing dissidents is that it creates more dissidents. Enough dissidents and they can create their own calendar, which gives them different magic powers and endangers the empire. Enough adherence to a heretical calendar threatens the official one and causes ‘calendrical rot’, a weakening of the strength of the calendar.

Did that make any sense? No? The point is, there’s a bunch of rules, some of them are horrible, and if not everyone follows the rules the magic stops working. Got it? Cool. The implications of this are things like democracy itself being considered heretical, and state controlled magic used to force loyalty on a massive scale.
Someday someone might come up with a better government, one in which brainwashing and the remembrances’ ritual torture weren’t an unremarkable fact of life. Until then, he did what he could
Such fun!

Inevitably with such a complicated setting, things don’t quite feel like they make sense and you just trust that the author knows better than you. For example (spoilers where I briefly complain about the second book):

The second book hinges on creating a calendrical spike. This appears to mean ‘doing something so disruptive to the social order that the way magic works changes’. It took me a while to work that out. The way Cheris does this is by murdering a bunch of military commanders. The military commanders aren’t very nice, so I was in full support of this. However, Mikodez simultaneously murders five of the six Hexarchate rulers. Shouldn’t that also be a calendrical spike? I don’t know. I don’t know why I try to understand this. It’s better if I just trust in Cheris’ fabulous mathematical skills.

I know I got a little distracted spending this whole review talking about the magic system, but the characters are great too. You never know if any of the POV characters are telling the truth, because they’re all very sneaky. Unreliable narrators are cool when you write them well, and it’s managed here. One of them is sort of a really smart force ghost, and our main character Cheris has to try and get their help but also make sure they don’t do a (second) mass killing. Mikodez is a wise-cracking ministry leader with a reputation for assassinating his own people. There are also these lovely lil robot fellas, who have strong opinions about courtesy and are total nerds. They take the form of animals; the reason for this is unclear, maybe they just like it. You might think that characters would be overshadowed by the bizarre universe that they’ve been placed in, but it just allows you to focus on them. Among the madness and the maths, there are these truly human people living as best they can.

Lee’s approach to structure and prose feels unique as well. There are quite a few space battles in this story, it being a space opera. In my short form reviews, I’ve mentioned a lot how writers can be skilled at making combat feel brutal and violent. Lee has gone in the other direction, using symbolism and the strange, strange magic system to turn battles and death into something thick with beauty and grace. In all, it’s a very odd book. But a very good one.
Yours in calendrical heresy,
ML

quote: Numbers could move hearts, with the right numbers, and with the right hearts.
alt: So imagine a vertical disc, but the top half is a really spiky sphere. And it's a bit on fire. And it's a space station. This cover is hard to explain, I'm afraid.

title: Gideon the Ninth
summary: Gay necromancers repeatedly break your heart

content.value: Set in a world where everyone is a lesbian, God is called John, and 'immortal death magician' is a valid career path, we play Among Us in a haunted palace.

This series is very, very good. It's very very, painful. I possibly should have expected this from a book about necromancers, but I was caught slightly off guard by how my heart has been torn to shreds. Which some of the characters could empathise with in a slightly more literal sense.
Gideon marveled that someone could live in the universe only seventeen years and yet wear black and sneer with such ancient self-assurance.

Gideon grew up with a bunch of death cultists and one surprisingly normal sword-master. Somehow, this resulted in her having the vocabulary of a modern day teenager. The narration is consistently sarcastic and full of attitude, no matter how grave the current situation is. I am a fan of this kind of voice, but I can see that it might not be everyone’s favourite (see also: Shallan).
Harrow is a necromancer, who can do terrifying things with bones and doesn't care about your feelings. They hate each other. And also definitely love each other. #griddlehark.

The other characters are quite the menagerie. Some of them talk like you would actually expect necromancers with thousands of years of tradition behind them to talk, and some of them feel like totally normal people who happen to have death magic and/or swords. There are quite a few that are all dropped on you at the same time, and I had a hard time keeping track. There’s a convenient list at the start of the book. We get to know them all slowly over the course of the book, as Muir insidiously gets you attached to them. And then makes them feel pain. Thanks, Muir.

You’re going to die spewing your own lungs out of your nostrils, having failed at the finish line because you couldn’t help but prattle about why you killed innocent people, as though your reasons were interesting …

The plot is not the book’s strength. It’s ostensibly some kind of mystery, but it's a little all over the place. It was all a bit chaotic, but the chaos felt justified. What else would happen if you threw a bunch of necromancers into a haunted palace? The strength of the plot comes from the characters and their relationships. While the plot wasn’t impressive on it’s own, what it did to the characters had me gripped.

The second book has a far closer focus on the plot side of things. The first 60% makes very little sense, but that percentage can drop significantly depending when you work out what's happening. I'm a big fan of the mysteries and payoff the sequel. It's also a
very
different vibe, far more psychological and grim.
Thalergenic planets may be converted to be thanergy planets, i.e, dying planets, but almost never thanergenic (producing death energy but on a stable basis).

This is not a book for people who like thorough sci-fi worldbuilding, but it is absolutely one for people who like the nitty-gritty of magic systems. Muir takes the increasingly popular sciency magic approach, and Gideon regularly finds herself listening to necromancers jabber about 'thalurgy' or 'topological resonance'. If you’re concentrating, you can understand what they’re talking about. I took more the same approach as Gideon and understood it insofar as was necessary. If you're willing to wait until the second book, a lot more worldbuilding gets done.
Maybe it's that I find the idea comforting...that thousands of years after you're gone...is when you really live. That your echo is louder than your voice is.

When not directly tied to Gideon’s narration, the prose is lovely. Muir’s combat particularly shines - Gideon is not unaware of the horror of violence, but also enthralled. The beauty and terror is communicated wonderfully through prose. Gideon herself tends to say things like ‘Harrow slithered more deeply underneath the covers like a bad dark snake’, which is hilarious but could not be called beautiful. Gideon entirely lacks contextual awareness and her irreverent, sarcastic wit is woven throughout the book. It's great fun as long as you like her humour. It's worth noting that in the second book, the narration is very different. The humour is still there, but it's not as in-your-face.
If you're a fan of magic systems, necromancers, hilarious narrators or emotional trauma, this book is for you.

quote: I pray that which was buried remains buried, insensate, in perpetual rest, with closed eye and stilled brain.
alt: Pictured is a woman with skull facepaint and flaring red hair. Her clothes are black and ragged. They're holding their sword out to the side and are wearing some 'worryingly fly sunglasses' (words of the author). They are surrounded by pieces of human skeletons, flying through the air. Their sword is red with blood, and their off hand has been impaled by one of the pieces of bone.

title: A Memory Called Empire
summary: A beautiful exploration of an intoxicating foreign culture.

content.value: A beautiful exploration of an intoxicating foreign culture. Teixcalaan is a fabulously romantic scifi setting, with influences from Byzantium to Mesoamerica. Literature and politics are often one and the same, and the society is full of tantalising allusions and literary references.  Set in this luscious landscape is a gripping political drama, with sharply intelligent characters to take you along for the ride. While the book is scifi, the emphasis is placed not on technology or spaceships. The focus is on language, translation, and cultural exchange. Martin Cahill of TOR.com is a writer and so expressed it better than I ever could: 'it left me breathless with awe, this book that so effortlessly balances being a high-octane, science fiction action thriller, while also simultaneously being a thoughtful, complicated examination of identity, language, personhood, and truth.'
“How nice for us, that everyone lies,” Three Seagrass said cheerfully.
“Cultural exchange by mutually beneficial deception.” said Mahit.

The characters in this book are brilliant. Mahit is a very solid POV character, enthralled in the sweepingly enticing society of Teixcalaan along with us. Three Seagrass is possibly my favourite character ever. She’s wonderful, frighteningly smart, cuttingly funny. She is introduced to us as Mahit’s cultural liaison, to be the bridge between Mahit and Teixcalaan. This she does fabulously, despite Mahit getting them in the middle of a succession crisis. The only person in the book more competent is Nineteen Adze, who is so scary that she comes with her own epithet (she whose gracious presence illuminates the room like the edgeshine of a knife).

She’d spent half her life studying Teixcalaanli literature and she was just barely good enough to follow this game, recognize a few of the referents. If she tried herself she’d—oh, they wouldn’t laugh. They’d be indulgent. Indulgent of the poor, ignorant barbarian playing so hard at civilization

Teixcalaan is a pleasingly unique sci-fi experience. The focus of the series is so strongly on culture that the setting had to shine - and it does. Martine drew inspiration from a lot of sources - the pervasive expansion from American imperialism, the religion and aesthetics from the Mexica, the empire and literature from Byzantium. Teixcalaan believes that it is the centre of the universe, and anything outside it is uncivilised, barbarian. Teixcalaan’s body of literature is a foundational part of their society. The consequence of this is that Teixcalaan is both trapped and empowered by it’s literary tradition, formed and crafted by it’s history. That’s why it’s
A Memory Called Empire

. The strength of this cultural memory is a significant part of what makes Teixcalaan so powerful. The thematic power of a society built around stories carries it’s ideas beyond its borders, and makes being a citizen intoxicatingly attractive for non-citizens. I was certainly won over. Mahit struggles with this throughout the book, wishing so badly to be part of this beautiful, complex, tantalisingly exclusionary society.
The word for “world” and the word for “the City” were the same, as was the word for “empire.” It was impossible to specify.

The plot is that of a political drama, as Mahit attempts to stop the might of Teixcalaan from subsuming her home, and also gets entirely sidetracked by Teixcalaan’s succession crisis. There are an awful lot of characters and motivations in play. I pretty much understand what’s happening now that I’ve read it three times. Every turn in the plot feels deliciously justified, and never takes a breath - the whole book is at a breakneck pace. I was exhausted by the end from following it, complex but thrilling, and impossible to put down. The finale is immensely satisfying and achingly incomplete all at once.
Perhaps succor was enough to keep a whole population trapped, willingly.

Martine’s prose is perfectly acceptable, but nothing stellar. I would prefer a little more show and a little less tell, particularly at the start, but everything else is so perfect that I really don’t mind. Mahit’s struggle to adapt to the society is portrayed very well, and her linguistic and cultural observations are great (she’s such a nerd). The poetry in-world is meant to be all fancy, with complex meters and rhyming schemes. Martine made the probably good choice not to attempt to replicate this, but instead to ‘
gesture
at poetry instead of trying to achieve the heights of the form’. Hence, the poetry in the books is pleasant but not particularly exciting.
If you’re a fan of political drama, enthralling cultures, intelligent characters or linguistic trivia, this book is for you.

quote: Perhaps succor was enough to keep a whole population trapped, willingly.
alt: The front cover of A Memory Called Empire, which is a beautiful and aw-inspiring depiction of the main character standing in front of the sun throne - futuristic and blocky with a spiked semicircle reminiscent of the sun behind it. The largest spikes would be at least ten meters. It's representative of the ideals of Teixcalaan, imposing, artistic, luxurious.

title: Malazan Book of the Fallen
summary: A weave of a thousand tragic histories

content.value: The book of the fallen

is a long series. And yet every line suggests to you that there could have been a thousand more books covering a thousand years of tragedy. Every race, every god, every city, has depths to them that the reader can never really discover, merely feel a sense of awe and vertigo at Erikson's skill in mythological worldbuilding that has not been seen since Tolkien. It's not always an easy series to read
many of the books would be well described as tragedies

but the grief is interspersed with flashes of Pratchett-like absurdity in the prose and characters. You're also repeatedly thrown in the deep end; Erikson does not believe in holding the reader's hand, and you will often spend the first part of a book getting your bearings. But trust me, it's worth it. I agree completely with
this
review from Salon, so go and look at that if you aren't convinced.

quote: That's a succinct summary of humankind, I'd say. Who needs tomes and volumes of history? Children are dying. The injustices of the world hide in those three words
alt: The cover of the Malazan complete edition. A huge city hovers in the air, crows wheeling around it. The air is thick with yellow smoke, and buildings burn on the ground. A woman with long blond hair stand in the foreground, looking up at the looming city.

title: Among Others
summary: A quiet bookish book with magic around the edges

content.value: Among Others is not the type of book you expect to win the Hugo
and

Nebula. Most of the plot happened before the book started. They saved the world, and her twin sister died, whose presence is most felt in between the lines, in the holes she would have filled. Because of this the book has moments of aching grief, but there are more that are of hope. There’s very little plot left for the actual book; Mor is mostly interested in reading speculative fiction and trying to lead a good life (which describes me also).

Although largely being set in normal 1979 England, the book has magic all around the edges. The magic is quiet and unknowable. There’s a depiction of fairies that I loved — I don’t know much about traditional folklore so I’m not sure how directly inspired it is, but they’re the most
fae

fairies I think I’ve seen. They’re very definitely unhuman, and tend to have conversations without nouns in them (or without words at all). Mor herself is a girl with a matter-of-fact view of life who’s trying to balance a book club, a boarding school, and an… evil witch mother? The mother doesn’t really feature that heavily, and I would argue she’s intended to be a ‘storybook villain’ of sorts for Mor. Mor’s injured leg feels like more of a villain most of the time.
This is a book by, for, and about readers. Aside from the incomprehensible decision for her dad to do something upsetting that had no bearing on the rest of the book, it’s lovely.

quote: It doesn't matter. I have books, new books, and I can bear anything as long as there are books.
alt: A girl reads a book in the sun. It's realistic, and feels like a picnic on a summer's day.

title: Babel, Or the Necessity of Violence
summary: A fiercely anti-colonial take on dark academia

content.value: This book was
almost

great. The setting is as well executed as you would expect, Kuang herself having studied in Oxford as a Chinese immigrant, like our protagonist. The story, setting, and magic system are based around linguistics and translation, and I loved them, but these are only vehicles for the book’s main point, that being anti-colonialism. I have no problems with this in general, but I do not like how Kuang executed it. British imperialism and aggressive anti-colonialism are covered in three ways. First, the character’s experiences and the plot of the book focus quite closely on these concepts. This was fine. My problems lie in the other two angles of approach. In the prose was regularly interspersed narration that was quite clearly not from the POV character, but rather Kuang herself making some arch comment about injustice. Second, there were footnotes, which were occasionally used to cite sources (in a fiction novel??) or provide translations (this was good actually) or for
more

pointed anti-colonialist comments. It’s the most heavy handed approach I’ve ever seen from anyone writing anything, never mind someone with the literary chops of Kuang. It feels, and I am glad to find I am not alone in this feeling, that she is treating her audience like idiots. It got in the way of the actual book, which, again, I actually quite liked. Fortunately, she mostly stopped doing this towards the end of the book when the actual content was picking up. A very frustrating read, but still worth it, particularly if you don’t think you’ll be annoyed by my complaints. It wanted to be dark academia in the way it should be done, and it’s
so
close.

quote: That's just what translation is, I think. That's all speaking is. Listening to the other and trying to see past your own biases to glimpse what they're trying to say. Showing yourself to the world, and hoping someone else understands.
alt: Black and white imagery of the titular Babel, a college in a fictional Oxford. It towers grandly over the rest of the city, and birds spiral their way up to the top.

title: Tomorrow, and Tomorrow, and Tomorrow
summary: A book about art, love, and video games.

content.value: I don’t read much that isn’t SFF. Every review I have made on this site to date is a speculative fiction novel. I thought I would give this one a go, because John Green recommended it, and it’s about video games, and I like John Green and video games. As it turns out, it’s a lot more ‘John Green’ than video games. The book would, I think, might mean less to someone who has never experienced the wonder of a game that feels like it was designed just for them. On the other hand, that’s not really what it’s about. It’s mostly about art, about humans, about
us

. It’s about three people trying to create meaning, and have relationships, and live a life, even when it’s difficult. It’s about when loving is too hard, and when it’s too easy, and what you do when it’s gone. It’s not a happy book, but it’s heartbreakingly hopeful. It’s not perfect — it really only picked up at the end, which itself was perhaps more indulgent than I’d like, but this is a case where the imperfections don’t take away from the greater work. Sadie and Sam are written as humanly as I’ve ever seen, and while Marx is too perfect to be real, you can’t help but love him (people always talk about the book as if it’s just about Sadie and Sam; I find this insulting). It’s a lovely book, as long as you read through the parts where it isn’t.

quote: What is a game?" Marx said. "It's tomorrow, and tomorrow, and tomorrow. It's the possibility of infinite rebirth, infinite redemption. The idea that if you keep playing, you could win. No loss is permanent, because nothing is permanent, ever.
alt: The Great Wave off Kanagawa is one of the most iconic pieces of art in the world, a stylised print of a towering wave. In this cover it sits behind the title of the book rendered in 3D rainbow toned text. At the bottom John Green says it is one of the greatest books he has ever read.

title: Perdido Street Station
summary: An endlessly inventive triumph of weird fiction.

content.value: China Miéville’s writing is part of a movement referred to as ‘new weird’, a genre which is hard to pin down. It sometimes refers to the use of realistic, urban settings as a base for more speculative elements, or the melding of a range of genres and sources. Perdido Street Station’s setting is an eclectic mix of steampunk, urban fantasy, horror, and political fiction. One of our protagonists is a scientist, who trades in a compelling mix of recognisable concepts and thoroughly developed speculative ones. There are a multitude of non-human races present, and none of them are those you’d expect to find — we’ve got cactus people, interdimensional spider aestheticists, and a secret group of disembodied hands. They all live in a sprawling industrial city, their fabulousness only footnotes to the struggles of everyday life. Miéville is an outspoken leftist, and is not afraid to communicate that overtly through his fiction. The tone is quite dark and often almost angry — he is not afraid to take us to grim places. The plot isn’t the strongest: deus ex machina is more a matter of course in such a strange world. I was perfectly happy to luxuriate in the wonderful setting and characters Miéville presents.

quote: The great variegated fortress of dark brick and scrubbed concrete and wood and steel and stone, the edifice that yawned hugely at the city's vulgar heart, Perdido Street Station.
alt: 'Flawlessly plotted and relentlessly, stunningly inventive: a conceptual breakthrough of the highest order', says Kirkus Reviews. Sometimes I wonder why I write reviews when other people are so eloquent. The center of the cover is a moth, with out of focus, dilapidated city blocks in the background.

title: The Poppy War
summary: An emotionally traumatic fantasy reprise of the Second Sino-Japanese War.

content.value: This book starts quite tropey and predictable, but manages to mostly escape this feeling as the book and the series go on. It’s honestly difficult for me to remember what happened in the first book, because my main impression of the series is the pain the later books caused me. This is not a happy and fun series. It will hurt you. The portrayal of warfare and its consequences is brutal and unflinching. The fact that it’s based on real life events makes it only all the more terrifying. There’s a lot of scheming and politics and such as well. Essentially the book is about the fate of a nation, as it tears itself apart from the inside and faces threats from without. Our main characters are very much antiheroes, so that most of the time you’re not entirely sure whether you should be cheering or not. They are also complex, with long and sometimes surprising character arcs. Something Kuang does particularly well is the fight scenes, allowing them to feel tense and bloody. This is not a series for the faint-hearted, but it does nail what it’s going for.

quote: War doesn't determine who's right. War determines who remains.
alt: The cover of The Poppy War, an ink drawing of an archer with their bow strung. As an ink drawing it's grayscale, so it sacrifices detail for starkness, turning it from art into symbolism.

title: The Collapsing Empire
summary: Easy to read and good sci-fi fun

content.value: John Scalzi has the marvellous talent of being able to write seemingly whatever he wants and making it seem cohesive. Parts of this book (more so with the sequels) feel less polished or more random than you might expect, but this is a worthy cost of writing such a fun story. It feels more like a surprisingly high quality AO3 story than a novel that was part of a multi-million dollar deal, but somehow it works. The characters mostly have the same personality. I’m ok with that, because the personality is “being hilarious”. Scalzi has a talent for conversational, wise-cracking, charismatic narration which is really what makes the book. The story has Dune vibes in that we have great houses competing as the world falls apart around them. However, it’s far more accessible than Dune, far more well paced and in my opinion far more enjoyable. What’s happening is essentially the method of travelling between planets is going to stop working, which has concerning supply line implications (imagine if the shipping stopped working) but many people refuse to believe in this impending natural catastrophe (sound familiar?). This novel is just a good time.

quote: In the Interdependency, with its ethos of interconnectedness combined with a guild-centered, monopolistic economy, they’d created possibly the most ridiculously complex method of ensuring the survival of the species they could have devised.
alt: The cover of The Collapsing Empire, which appears to be the spaceship equivalent of an aircraft carrier. It's covered in grass fields, and smaller spaceships are launching from it. It's very cinematic, a classic epic sci-fi feeling.

title: Jade City
summary: The Godfather with magic and kung fu

content.value: The author compares these books to The Godfather and says it’s inspired by wuxia and gangster movies. It’s certainly evidence that there’s always more to explore in the fantasy genre. It starts a bit slow, but the tension and violence ramps up throughout. The characterisations are such that you oscillate between hating and loving your main cast. Loving them turns out to be a mistake, as Lee puts them through pain and heartbreak ruthlessly. She has no qualms about killing off her characters — in fact I’d prefer it happened a little less. There’s only so much my heart can take! The story is centred around the conflict between two ancient clans, which creates plenty of intrigue and politics as well as the traditional martial arts duels. Lee is good at writing fights
(she does have multiple black belts)

where the action feels intensely violent despite the superhuman abilities of the characters. If you like morally grey characters, Hong Kong gangster films, or stories about family and brotherhood, give it a go.

quote: The clan is my blood and the pillar it’s master. On my honor, on my life, on my jade.

title: Hyperion
summary: A classic sci-fi novel with serious thematic weight.

content.value: I don’t read many old books. Well, old is a strong word, Hyperion was published in 1989. I don’t read many books that weren’t published this century. When I do, I often find they haven’t really stood up to the fiction I’m reading right now, presumably because they were produced for a different audience with a different context, inspired by the style of a different body of work. Hyperion, however, stood up. I finished the Cantos feeling like it had almost religious significance, and indeed religion or the lack of it is one of the main themes. The story is about a pilgrimage, and there’s enough characters introduced simultaneously that I found it very confusing for a while, but fear not! All characters are fully individual and we learn about each of them through flashbacks. The structure of the novel is one of its main strengths, using a combination of the pilgrimage and flashbacks to weave some fabulously rich themes and symbolism into a cohesive story. What’s interesting about the flashbacks is the tonal shift for each of them — one of them even switching genre entirely. This is less a space opera and more a sci-fi in the tradition of Asimov; Massive, imposing, and deeply meaningful.

quote: Words bend our thinking to infinite paths of self-delusion, and the fact that we spend most of our mental lives in brain mansions built of words means that we lack the objectivity necessary to see the terrible distortion of reality which language brings.
alt: The cover for the Hyperion Omnibus, an imposing spiked metal helmet in front of a starry background. Peter Hamilton says it 'Sets the standard for SF in the new century' which is odd because it was published relatively near the end of last century.

title: The Expanse
summary: A space opera for the modern day

content.value: I finished this series feeling less like I had completed a work of fiction and more like I had just experienced a possible future. Corey succeeded in creating a world with so much depth and so many layers that it’s more believable than any other speculative fiction world I’ve read. Somehow the scope gets bigger every book, despite me feeling like that isn’t possible at the end of each one. The plots really are quite amazing, building on each previous book with overarching storylines,  and they let the characters shine. You get some horror and mystery elements, a bunch of traditional hard sci-fi spaceship stuff, and a fair few space battles. Not only is that genre stuff done well, but the friendship and dynamics of the small crew that we follow are excellent in their own right. Do you love Star Wars but wish it took itself more seriously? Did you love Foundation and want to experience that feeling again? Here’s your space opera for the modern day.

quote: Earthers get to walk outside into the light, breathe pure air, look up at a blue sky, and see something that gives them hope. And what do they do? They look past that light, past that blue sky. They see the stars, and they think, 'Mine.'
alt: A spaceship sits in front of mars, backlit by the sun. It's meant to inspire awe through it's scale and beauty.

title: The Unspoken Name
summary: Attempted fantasy novel gets distracted by a gay love story

content.value: The book opens with our orc protagonist being raised by a death cult, and continues with her becoming an assassin for a wizard. Don’t tell me that doesn’t sound like a good time. That was Csorwe, our badass POV, who we follow along with Tal, a swordsman with a bad attitude. They both serve Sethennai, a wizard who orders them around with increasingly suspect morals and concerning father-figure dynamics. We also meet Qanwa, another magician who is trying not to be taken over by her fire god and struggling against her ordained future. The setting is cool but not really the focus — Larkwood allows fantastical elements to exist without needing full explanations. This allows the focus to be on the relationships, which are conflicted and painful and confusing. Still, there’s a wide range of cultures, nations, and gods for those who read fantasy for the fantastical. All the characters I mentioned are queer, but you couldn’t really call it a queer story, that’s just who they are. Read this book for the wonderful disaster characters and their attempts to have functional relationships.

quote: She told him the plan. It was loud and dumb and very likely to hurt, so, of course, he agreed.
alt: The cover of The Unspoken Name. A horn with bands of gold lies on charcoal. Sparks float across the page.

title: Project Hail Mary
summary: A hilarious and hopeful sci-fi (emphasis on sci) adventure

content.value: I'm one of those rare people who liked Artemis more than The Martian, and this book takes the best of both worlds. Weir is great at writing accessible hard fantasy, and this book gives him lots of opportunities to flex his science communication skills. As with The Martian, you don’t need to follow all the science jabber to have fun. The main character has essentially the same personality as the dude from The Martian, but that’s ok because Weir writes that person very well. They’re sassy and sarcastic and intelligent, a joy to read. He starts having lost his memory and gains it back over time, which is a plot device we’ve all seen before but nevertheless does its job. He regains his memory through flashbacks to Earth, which he is on a mission to save. There’s a supporting character who I won’t tell you about but they are wonderful. A lot of the book is essentially the relationship between these unlikely friends. With a bunch of science, of course! The ending felt vaguely unsatisfactory to me (which I’ve seen some people echo) but the book was otherwise almost perfect.

quote: But I have to save humanity first. Stupid humanity. Getting in the way of my hobbies.
alt: An astronaut floats in space, attached to a tether which runs off page. It looks somewhat unsafe.

title: Ten Thousand Doors of January
summary: A thoroughly bookish adventure

content.value: This is a book for readers. It’s a story about stories, and about love, and the narrator allows us to be delightfully complicit in the narrative indulgence. It’s a portal fantasy, so we see our protagonists venture through a variety of worlds through Doors, the pathways across reality. The prose is wonderful — whimsical, poetic, and almost talkative. We follow January, a young girl who dreams of adventure and of course finds one. She strives to escape the patriarchal secret society which is seeking to impose order and stagnation on the world. In her friends and her travels she finds love and hope, the danger and the beauty of stories. Harrow explores race, sexism, colonialism and more. It’s a story which is unlikely to surprise you but will leave you satisfied and perhaps understood.

quote: I hope you will find the cracks in the world and wedge them wider, so the light of other suns shines through; I hope you will keep the world unruly, messy, full of strange magics; I hope you will run through every open Door and tell stories when you return
alt: This is such a pretty cover! It's got flowers all around the edges and some sort of gold... thing in the middle. I'm going to guess it's a gold mirror with a fancy border but really it's just a nice design. The title of the book is written in a different fancy font for each word.

title: Ministry for the Future
summary: A story of humanity and our self-imposed climate struggle

content.value: This is not the type of story I normally read, possibly because it’s not the type of story people normally write. It’s an optimistic story about humanity's struggle and eventual success (ish) to combat climate change. The story is interspersed with essays, notes, and narratives of various forms from inside the world. We see economic, scientific and personal battles along the way. As a narrative it’s pretty good, although towards the end it began to feel a bit weaker. However, the focus isn’t really on the narrative. It feels more like a sociological hypothesis, an attempt to predict the course of human history. People do this all the time of course, but rarely do they do it with such engaging prose and characters. The book will either turn out to be stunningly prescient or a cute example of leftist optimism. We can but hope.

quote: Ideology, n. An imaginary relationship to a real situation.  In common usage, what the other person has, especially when systematically distorting the facts.
alt: A human stands in the body of an airship, looking into a blue sky with another airship hanging in the air. It feels futuristic and hopeful.

title: Powder Mage Trilogy
summary: A thrilling napoleonic military fantasy.

content.value: It's tough to find fantasy set in this era - what seems to be known as "flintlock fantasy" - but McClellan has provided a superb modern example. The series opens with a coup and proceeds to explore the geopolitical consequences. Being a military fantasy, we follow armies and battles a fair amount. Similarly, fighting and particularly gunfights are common, and I know this is an odd thing to say but McClellan writes guns
well

. It’s hard to explain that one, so you’ll just have to read the book. I know there’s an audience which will love the idea of napoleonic fantasy, and here’s your book! It’s important to note however that this is by no means the only reason to read them. The characters, their relationships, and international intrigue are the reason the military sections are engaging. There’s three neat magic systems and a bunch of great characters to get to know.

quote: The age of kings is dead, and I have killed it.
alt: The cover of Promise of Blood. We see an older soldier who looks a bit roughed up sitting in a throne. A rifle rests across his lap. There's a crown in a puddle of blood on the floor. I think you can grasp the implication...

title: The Stormlight Archive
summary: The premier modern epic.

content.value: The Stormlight Archive is my favourite series. It's a story that is unrepentantly epic. Sanderson's worldbuilding is unparalleled, with an ability to craft worlds like no one else. The magic system in typical Sanderson fashion is as developed as a science. The plot is everything you could hope for from an epic fantasy series, with an ambitious scope and intricate threads underpinning every development. Although the cast is as large as it is diverse, each book focuses on an individual, making them intense character studies so that it's impossible to avoid falling in love with each main character. His prose is far more accessible than you would typically find in this genre, with solid pacing and a rare lack of over description. These are only some of the things making this series one of the most popular modern fantasy series. Brandon Sanderson is this generation's Tolkein, Jordan or Martin, and this is his magnum opus.

quote: Honour is dead. But I'll see what I can do.
alt: The covers of the first four Stormlight books, which I am now going to describe in far too much detail. They are all stark and stylised, designed with a limited but striking palette, only red, black and white. They all have a large, perfectly circular red sun in the background, which is the only colour except touches of red elsewhere. The first is the upper body of a knight, with their visor up. Stormlight is rising from their helmet and sword, and they are weary but ready to fight on. The second shows a man (Kaladin?)with a spear and ornate armour, with a long cloak caught by the wind, flaring to their side. The third shows Jasnah, glaring at the camera holding her sword to her side, like the absolute badass she is. Smoke is drifting behind her, and rough rocks are in the foreground. The final cover is Shallan, holding a very long, thing sword, in a dress that she really shouldn't be fighting in. There are some quite nice white blossoms at the top, and more of those rocks at the bottom. This description is possibly longer than the review.

title: Wayfarers
summary: The quintessential feel-good sci-fi.

content.value: The Wayfarers series by Becky Chambers is a story that is heart-warming but not lacking in complexity. Every character is indescribably human (even when they're an alien), and the societies and communities described are unique, deep, and usually incredibly wholesome. The socialist community spirit found in the Exodan Fleet especially won my heart. The stories are on the whole mild, thoughtful, but their social commentaries and explorations of the human (and alien) experience are no less powerful for it. The focus is heavily on the characters, driven by their cultures and personalities. There is very little action, preferring to look at interpersonal and everyday problems. The term 'comfort sci-fi' has never been quite so applicable.

quote: I can wait for the galaxy outside to get a little kinder.
alt: The cover of each book in the Wayfarers series. They picture a small silhoutted figure (or figures) at the bottom on silhouetted terrain. They're looking up at a nighttime galaxy awash with colour. The figures look lonely, or possibly contemplative, but the sky is beautiful. An image of aching contrast.

title: The Masquerade
summary: Geopolitcal, heart-wrenching journey into an inexorable colonial power.

content.value: The Masquerade by Seth Dickinson follows Baru Cormorant, who I would really prefer not to follow but also can't look away. It's a stunning criticism of... pretty much everything. Colonialism, homophobia, transphobia, capitalism, racism - you name it, it's covered. The society providing the backdrop for this plethora of thematic messaging is Imperial Falcrest, one of the most intriguing fantasy cultures I've read - subtle, inexorable, cunning. It uses indoctrination, assimilation and economics to achieve its objectives. The series revolves around Baru's quest to destroy it from the inside while trying not to become a monster herself. Following Baru's increasingly unstable mental state, we are taken on a journey through economic machinations, geopolitics and revolution. The book didn't receive nearly as much acclaim as I think it deserves, with a lot of criticism around pacing and writing style (which is apparently 'Wikipedia style'), so bear that in mind. The climax of the first book left me heartbroken, and subsequent books left me both hating the books and loving them, feeling distinctly uncomfortable but still enthralled.

quote: This is the truth. You will know because it hurts.
alt: The cover of The Monster Baru Cormorant, which is an eery, smiling mask set aflame, crumbling, fire pouring out an eye. It's disturbing and symbolic, much like the book. The words 'Unmake the system' and 'Remake the world' are written below.

title: The Kingkiller Chronicles
summary: finish the series Rothfuss smh

content.value: The Kingkiller Chronicles are popularly known for both their fantastic prose, and how it's been ten thousand years and we still don't have the third book. Your opinion on Rothfuss's writing speed notwithstanding, he has an undeniable talent for poetic writing and the ability to craft a world that feels both unknowable and fully realised. It follows the main character from their childhood onwards, from their desperate struggle against poverty to increasingly fantastical shenanigans. Rothfuss is a perfectionist, which is very apparent when reading - everything feels very intentional, the descriptions and foreshadowing are perfectly placed. It's entirely based around the character of Kvothe, so if you don't like his arrogant, flamboyant approach to life, the series may be hard for you. The second book is not nearly as good, with a lack of direction and...
that
scene. Yeah. No.

quote: Words can light fires in the minds of men. Words can wring tears from the hardest hearts.
alt: The cover of The Name of the Wind, the first book in the series. The name of the book and auther are depicted in a font with leafy, floral designs. In the center there is what appears to be Chancellor Palpatine, but probably isn't. It's a person wearing a black coat with a cowl, so you cannot see above their nose. What you can see is chalk white, with a slight sinister red glow coming from the hood where eyes probably are. They are framed by vines and trees.

title: Discworld
summary: Absurdist comedic fantasy that is also serious political commentary

content.value: I'm mildly reluctant to review the Discworld because its deceptive intelligence and subversive approach to fantasy makes it hard to articulate why it's so wonderful. Pratchett crafted a personality for his books, and this along with his extraordinary skill in writing absurdist comedic fantasy that is also serious political commentary are only part of what's made it such an iconic series. The execution of what Pratchett was trying to achieve is near-perfect, and though the books won't be for everyone, there's nothing I think he could have done better. The sheer audacity to personify death as a mildly reluctant civil servant and make me love them? The man's a genius. There's some disagreement about where to start the series, the only consistent recommendation being 'not the start', which I agree with. I recommend the Witches series or Small Gods for a stand-alone.

quote: Odd thing, ain't it... you meet people one at a time, they seem decent, they got brains that work, and then they get together and you hear the voice of the people. And it snarls.
alt: A piece of fanart depicting the many odd characters of the discworld. It's like a movie poster, although I'm not sure that is very helpful to the audience of alt-text. Just imagine a bunch of wacky people and a grim reaper.

title: Murderbot
summary: The softest and most fluffy death robot you'll ever meet.

content.value: Murderbot is the softest and most humane robot you'll ever meet. Mentally, that is. Physically, they have guns in their arms. The series is not just character-driven, but is almost a character study of Murderbot's psychology, history, and relationships. Through the first four novellas and subsequent novels, I cannot imagine a reader not falling in love with them.  It's pleasantly funny without being light-hearted, carefully handling Murderbot's mental health issues and especially social anxiety. That is correct, we are talking about a death robot with social anxiety. The setting is a dystopia of space capitalism, and the plot involves a lot of working out what the evil corporations are up to and stopping them (mainly to save friends rather than anti-capitalist sentiment, although that is also there). The action scenes are some of my favourites, with Murderbot's unique voice and Wells's practical prose making them feel very much like action is happening.

quote: I was having an emotion, and I hate that
alt: The cover of the four Murderbot novellas, each of which features Murderbot, who looks sort of like someone in a cool spacesuit, along with traditional sci-fi imagery like space stations and starships.

title: The First Law
summary: The epitome of grimdark fantasy

content.value: Grimdark is becoming a more popular subgenre of fantasy, possibly because of all the G.R.R Martin fans starved for content. Joe Abercrombie is currently the strongest alternative, and in my opinion, does a far better job. If you're unfamiliar with the term 'grimdark', it's about what you'd expect - gritty, morally grey, characters keep dying on you. Abercrombie's masterful ability to develop interesting and consistent characters is his greatest skill and makes even the most distasteful characters engaging narrators. That's a good thing too, since even the 'good' characters are fundamentally flawed and I wouldn't like to meet any of them. All of the choices made are believable, giving the plot a character-driven feel despite how its mysteries and reveals are clearly well thought out. The books are also packed with grim humour, which I had great fun with. Abercrombie is so well placed to be a spiritual successor to GRRM that honestly just let him finish ASOIAF...

quote: People love to see death. It reminds them that however mean, however low, however horrible their lives become…at least they have one.
alt: The covers of four First Law books, which feature the title of each book with representations of characters from the book. The titles and art are stylised as if they had been done in ink, pure black and white with spots of ink scattered about.

title: Empress of Forever
summary: Another philosophical, quirky story from Max Gladstone

content.value: From Max Gladstone, author of the Craft Sequence's contract-law based magic system, comes another philosophical, quirky story. After the first section of the book, you might be thinking 'why am I reading about a Mary Sue in a fever dream' but it works out, I promise. The protagonist, Vivian Liao, is an obnoxiously intelligent tech entrepreneur who deals perfectly well with being teleported into an incomprehensible sci-fi setting because she's the type of genius that tech billionaires try to convince us they are. The story draws inspiration from various Chinese philosophies (particularly Journey to the West, I hear). A lot is going on, and it doesn't particularly care to slow down on our account, so it's marvelously complicated, imaginative and fast-paced. The characters are unique but universally lovable - from Hong, our loyal priest; to Zanj, who's 3000 years old and very angry.

quote: You’re not who you think you are,” Viv said. “You’re a dream. That’s all. But don’t take it too hard. So are the rest of us.
alt: Angry girl stares at us wearing a futuristic pointy metal hat. It looks cooler than it sounds, I promise.

title: Wayward Children
summary: Portal fantasy is alive and well.

content.value: Portal fantasies have been a staple of the fantasy genre for a long time. If you're unfamiliar, think Alice in Wonderland, or Narnia, or consult
TOR.com's convenient diagram

which sorts various worlds according to the Wayward Children's ordering system. Seanan McGuire's series is my favourite contemporary example of the genre. Her stories have the fairytale-like quality you would expect from children wandering into fantastical worlds, but they have sharp edges reminiscent of Grimms'. The plot leaves something to be desired; it's often meandering and dissatisfying, but that's possibly intentional. The focus is on the characters - who all need to feel as if they belong in another world, and McGuire creates this feeling perfectly. The characters are the most diverse cast I've ever seen, with a ranging cast of sexualities, genders, races and religions. If you like the sound of portal fantasy and don't mind a somewhat weak plot, give it a try!

quote: You’re nobody’s doorway but your own, and the only one who gets to tell you how your story ends is you.
alt: The first four books of the series, each picturing a unique doorway. The first - 'every heart a doorway' stands in a forest clearing, wooden, plain. The second - 'down among the sticks and bones' is a chest in a grey, rocky hillscape, a stunted, dead tree in the background. Doesn't look like much fun. The third is a door in reality itself, a shadow on the sky. The landscape is lurid colours, as if it were made of candy, as the title 'beneath a sugar sky' suggests. The last - 'in an absent dream' is in a tree, which is large and dark, creating a dimly lit, ominous scene.

title: The Broken Earth
summary: A wonderfully original approach to a large-scope fantasy series

content.value: This series by N.K Jemisin is a wonderfully original approach to a large-scope fantasy series. Jemisin is a very strong literary author, and this book like her other works is very well-rounded, with very few inconsistencies or weaknesses. The worldbuilding is fascinating, with a focus on geology and the manipulation or repercussions of it. The books focus on an impending apocalypse bought about by, well, the earth being broken. As I expect from a Jemisin novel, heavy topics and social commentary are tackled head-on. The characters are very sympathetic, with effective emotional prose driving home all the pain they're put through. There are passages of second person, which has had a mixed reception - I found it weird at first but got used to it quickly. The twists completely recontextualise the whole series a few times, which was very impressive. The final book was not quite the climax I had hoped for, but it was still a traumatically emotional finale

quote: For all those that have to fight for the respect that everyone else is given without question.
alt: The cover of The Fifth Season, the first book in the series, which really isn't very interesting and appears to be some masonry. SALON.com states 'one of the most celebrated new voices in fantasy' and the subtitle is 'every age must come to an end.'

title: Jonathan Strange & Mr Norrel
summary: The intersection between literary fiction and fantasy.

content.value: This tome of a book by Susanna Clarke is what I would describe as 'literary fantasy', set in (and in a style reminiscent of) 19th century England. Its greatest strength is its setting, an England which was long ago filled with magic. Magic is now relegated to 'theoretical magicians', who study it but cannot use it. This doesn't last long in the book, of course, and a delightfully fantastical depiction of historical England emerges. The prose is often flowery and the plot slow - early on we spend a painful amount of time doing nothing much. The narrator is presented to be a droll scholar of magic in the time and assumes we, too, are 19th century Englishmen. This is both a positive and negative, and the detailed footnotes and references to an imaginary body of literature enhance the atmosphere and immersion, but can sometimes get in the way. It's not to be understated, however, what a beautifully classical and nostalgically whimsical novel it is. The devious faeries, fickle magic and sly prose make this a book I adored.

quote: He understood for the first time that the world is not dumb at all, but merely waiting for someone to speak to it in a language it understands. In the fairy’s song the earth recognized the names by which it called itself.
alt: The first four books of the series, each picturing a unique doorway. The first - 'every heart a doorway' stands in a forest clearing, wooden, plain. The second - 'down among the sticks and bones' is a chest in a grey, rocky hillscape, a stunted, dead tree in the background. Doesn't look like much fun. The third is a door in reality itself, a shadow on the sky. The landscape is lurid colours, as if it were made of candy, as the title 'beneath a sugar sky' suggests.
